title: Data & Compute
oneLineScope: The corpora behind the first large language models — BooksCorpus, Wikipedia, WebText, C4 — and the compute story that connects them to scaling laws.
prose:
Where we are. Optimization and training dynamics described how gradients move through a transformer — the mechanics of a training step, learning-rate schedules, and what can go wrong. That node treated data as a given: sequences arrive, loss is computed, weights update. This node pulls back and asks what those sequences actually were: which corpora the landmark models trained on, how they were assembled and cleaned, and how much compute was required. These are not implementation details — the data choices and the compute regime were constitutive of what the first large models could do.

The gist. GPT-1, BERT, GPT-2, and T5 each trained on a different corpus: BooksCorpus, BooksCorpus plus Wikipedia, WebText, and C4 respectively. Across those four models, corpus size grew by roughly three orders of magnitude and cleaning infrastructure became a first-class engineering concern. Compute grew in parallel, from a few GPUs to clusters of TPUs, and a useful rule of thumb — \(C \approx 6ND\) — connects parameter count \(N\), training tokens \(D\), and total floating-point operations \(C\). The scaling laws node will quantify this appetite as a power law; this node lays out the empirical substrate those laws were measured against.

Why it matters. The transformer architecture and the pretraining objectives are elegant machinery. What drove that machinery to produce genuinely useful representations was text in industrial quantities and the compute to process it. Understanding where the data came from, how it was filtered, and what it cost to train on it is the prerequisite for reading the scaling-laws literature with full appreciation — and for understanding which aspects of early model behavior were architectural versus a function of what the model had seen.

The corpora

BooksCorpus (Zhu et al., 2015) was assembled to study cross-modal alignment — matching books with their film adaptations — but it became foundational to language model pretraining almost incidentally. The corpus consists of over 7,000 unpublished novels scraped from a self-publishing platform; Zhu et al. report approximately 800 million words. Two properties made it attractive beyond its size: the texts are long-form, with coherent narrative structure across thousands of tokens, providing exactly the kind of long-range dependency signal that short web snippets cannot; and the distribution of topics and register is relatively clean, since books that reach publication — even self-publication — tend toward grammatical prose. GPT-1 (Radford et al., 2018) was pretrained on BooksCorpus alone; BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) trained on BooksCorpus combined with English Wikipedia.

English Wikipedia, as used in BERT, contributed roughly 2.5 billion words at the time of training, per Devlin et al.'s description. Wikipedia text is clean, factual, and encyclopedic in register — a distributional profile quite different from novels. Combining it with BooksCorpus gave BERT both long-form narrative and structured factual text, which plausibly accounts for some of the breadth of what BERT’s representations encode. The combined corpus is modest by later standards — on the order of 3 billion words total — but it was sufficient to demonstrate that large-scale bidirectional pretraining produced representations competitive with or superior to task-specific architectures across many NLP benchmarks.

WebText was assembled for GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019). Rather than crawling the web indiscriminately, Radford et al. used a quality heuristic: they scraped all outbound links from Reddit posts that had received at least 3 upvotes. The intuition is that human curation — even the low bar of three Reddit upvotes — filters toward text someone found interesting or informative enough to share. The resulting corpus is approximately 40 GB of text (about 8 million documents), described by Radford et al. as WebText. This is considerably larger than BooksCorpus plus Wikipedia, and its web-native distribution — news, blogs, technical writing, fiction, forum posts — is closer to the range of text a general-purpose language model will encounter at inference. WebText is not publicly released; an approximate open recreation is called OpenWebText.

C4 — the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus — was constructed by Raffel et al. (2020) for T5. The starting point is Common Crawl, a publicly available, continuously updated crawl of the web that runs to petabytes of raw HTML. Common Crawl is enormous but extremely noisy: it contains deduplication artifacts, boilerplate, non-English text, and outright garbage. Raffel et al. applied a sequence of filters — removing pages without sentence-ending punctuation, deduplicating at the three-sentence-span level, discarding pages containing offensive language, keeping only English pages — to produce C4. After filtering, C4 is hundreds of gigabytes of text; Raffel et al. describe the English C4 as approximately 750 GB. Their §2 describes the filtering pipeline in careful detail and is worth reading for what it makes concrete: the vast majority of the raw web is discarded, and corpus quality is highly sensitive to which filters are applied and in what order.

The throughline across these four corpora is one of scale, diversity, and quality filtering. BooksCorpus: small, clean, long-form. Wikipedia: small, clean, factual. WebText: medium-sized, quality-heuristic-filtered web. C4: large, aggressively filtered web. Each step outward on the scale axis required new cleaning infrastructure. The community’s experience with C4 made clear that indiscriminate scaling — taking Common Crawl at face value — does not work. Deduplication and quality filtering are not preprocessing details; they materially affect downstream model behavior. A model trained on deduplicated data memorizes the training set less and generalizes better, a point that subsequent work (Hernandez et al. and Lee et al., among others) examined more carefully.

The compute story

Training these models moved from single-machine GPU runs to large multi-accelerator jobs during the GPT-1 to BERT to GPT-2 period. GPT-1 was trained on 8 GPUs; BERT was trained on 64 TPU v2 chips, as Devlin et al. describe in §3.1; GPT-2 required a compute cluster whose full specification Radford et al. do not publish in detail. The qualitative shift — from hardware a single researcher could plausibly rent to hardware requiring dedicated infrastructure — happened over roughly two years, 2018–2019.

A useful approximate relationship, introduced in Kaplan et al. (2020), connects total training compute \(C\) (in floating-point operations), parameter count \(N\), and training token count \(D\):

\[ C \approx 6 N D \]

The factor of 6 accounts for the forward pass, the backward pass (which is approximately twice the cost of the forward), and the parameter-update step; the derivation and the conditions under which this approximation holds are in Kaplan et al. §2.1. It is an approximation, not an identity: it ignores embedding layers and attention’s \(n^2\) term, which are sub-dominant for moderate sequence lengths and the dense transformer architectures of this era. But it is accurate to within a small constant for those architectures, and it is the right handle to reach for when reasoning about the order of magnitude of a training run from a paper’s reported parameter count and token count.

To put rough numbers to it — with the caveat that exact GPU-hours from these papers are not always published and the following are order-of-magnitude estimates derived from \(C \approx 6ND\) — a BERT-base model (\(N \approx 110\)M parameters, per Devlin et al.) trained on roughly 1 billion tokens implies \(C \approx 6 \times 1.1 \times 10^8 \times 10^9 \approx 6.6 \times 10^{17}\) FLOPs. GPT-2 (\(N \approx 1.5\)B, per Radford et al. 2019) on WebText’s roughly 10 billion tokens gives \(C \approx 9 \times 10^{19}\) FLOPs. These numbers are large but tractable on the hardware of the era. GPT-3 (\(N = 175\)B, \(D \approx 300\)B tokens, per Brown et al. 2020) pushed into the \(3 \times 10^{23}\) FLOP range — at that scale, compute cost, not algorithm design, became the binding constraint on experimentation.

Where it leads

The appetite of these models for unlabeled text and compute is precisely what scaling laws quantifies as a power law. The empirical observation that loss decreases predictably as \(N\), \(D\), and \(C\) grow — over many orders of magnitude, as Kaplan et al. show — gave the field a framework for planning training runs: given a fixed compute budget, how should it be split between a larger model and more data? The \(C \approx 6ND\) rule is the bridge between that question and the practical choices made in dataset construction and hardware allocation. The corpora and compute numbers in this node are the empirical substrate that makes those scaling curves meaningful; reading Kaplan et al. after this node, the axes of their graphs will have concrete referents.

Four datasets are marked as points or segments: BooksCorpus (~800M words, used by GPT-1 and BERT), English Wikipedia (~2.5B words, used by BERT), WebText (~40GB / ~8B tokens, used by GPT-2), and C4 (~750GB after filtering, used by T5). Each dataset label includes its source attribution. An annotation notes that C4 started from Common Crawl (petabytes) but was filtered down to hundreds of GB.

diagrams.caption: The pretraining pipeline: raw text passes through cleaning and deduplication, becomes a tokenized corpus, and feeds pretraining under a compute budget governed approximately by C ≈ 6ND.
diagrams.altText: A left-to-right pipeline with four stages. Stage 1: raw web and book text (labeled 'raw text'). Stage 2: a cleaning and deduplication box, annotated with example steps (language filter, deduplicate, quality filter). Stage 3: a tokenized corpus box, labeled with vocabulary size V and token count D. Stage 4: a pretraining box consuming compute C, with the approximation C ≈ 6ND labeled inside or beside it, and N (parameters) feeding in from below. An arrow from stage 4 leads to a trained model on the right.
diagrams.prompt: Conceptual pipeline diagram, left to right, with four labeled stages connected by arrows. Stage 1 (leftmost): a box or cloud labeled 'raw text' containing sub-labels 'web crawl', 'books', 'Wikipedia'. Stage 2: a box labeled 'cleaning & deduplication' with a short bulleted annotation listing example steps: language filter, deduplication, quality filter; annotate that this step is consequential, not cosmetic. Stage 3: a box labeled 'tokenized corpus' with sub-labels 'vocab size V' and 'token count D'. Stage 4: a box labeled 'pretraining' with the formula C ≈ 6ND written inside; an additional small box or arrow labeled 'model (N parameters)' feeds into this stage from below or the side. An arrow from stage 4 leads to a final box on the right labeled 'pretrained model'. Emphasize the cleaning step (stage 2) in red as the key quality gate; the tokenized corpus (stage 3) in blue as the thing under construction; the pretrained model output in green.

bibliography.citation: Zhu, Y., et al. (2015). "Aligning Books and Movies: Towards Story-Like Visual Explanations by Watching Movies and Reading Books." ICCV. arXiv:1506.06724.
bibliography.annotation: Source of BooksCorpus. §3.1 describes the corpus collection. The paper's primary goal is cross-modal alignment, not language modeling — the corpus became important incidentally. Cite for the ~800M-word figure and the long-form narrative property.

bibliography.citation: Radford, A., et al. (2019). "Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners." OpenAI Blog (GPT-2 paper).
bibliography.annotation: Source of the WebText corpus description: §2.2 describes the Reddit-link scraping heuristic, the ≥3 karma filter, and the ~40GB size. GPT-2 architecture and byte-level BPE tokenizer (V=50,257) are also described here.

bibliography.citation: Raffel, C., et al. (2020). "Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer." JMLR 21(140). arXiv:1910.10683.
bibliography.annotation: Source of C4 and the T5 model. §2 describes the full Common Crawl filtering pipeline in careful detail — the authoritative reference for what cleaning steps were applied, in what order, and why each matters. The paper also provides a systematic study of pretraining objectives and dataset choices.

bibliography.citation: Kaplan, J., et al. (2020). "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models." arXiv:2001.08361.
bibliography.annotation: Source of the C ≈ 6ND approximation (§2.1), including the derivation of the factor of 6 and the domain of validity. Also the primary source for the scaling-laws node; reading §2 alongside this node provides the bridge from corpus/compute facts to the empirical power-law framework.
